CIDB Registration G1 for Renovation Contractors Malaysia (2026)

Published 25 November 2026

CIDB registration is compulsory for renovation contractors in Malaysia: the CIDB Act requires anyone who carries out construction works, including repair and renovation, to register, and working without it carries a fine of RM10,000–100,000. Most small renovation firms start at grade G1, which covers contracts of up to RM200,000 each. A new G1 registration costs a RM50 processing fee plus a registration fee of RM20 a year, and is valid for up to 2 years.

This guide is general information, not legal advice. CIDB updates its requirements from time to time, so confirm your own position on the CIDB website or its CIMS portal before you apply.

Who needs CIDB registration

Section 25 of the Construction Industry Development Board Act 1994 (Act 520, amended in 2011) has required every contractor, local or foreign, to register with CIDB since 20 July 1995 before taking on construction work. CIDB’s definition of construction works is wide. It covers building, but also repair, maintenance, renewal, alteration, conversion, renovation and demolition. Hacking a bathroom, rebuilding a kitchen or fitting out a shop all fall inside it.

The Act lists some exemptions under Section 40(1), but CIDB’s registration page doesn’t spell them out, and none of the CIDB documents we reviewed sets a minimum job value below which you don’t need to register. If you think you’re exempt, get it confirmed by CIDB in writing.

It matters to your clients too. In 2024 CIDB’s chief executive warned that a homeowner who can’t show they appointed a contractor could be treated as the contractor themselves under Section 25. That’s one reason careful clients now ask for your registration number before they sign.

CIDB grades G1 to G7

Your grade sets the largest contract you may tender for or carry out. Taking a job above your grade’s limit, or outside your registered category, breaks the terms of your registration.

Grade Contract value limit Registration fee (CIDB) Minimum paid-up capital (reported)
G1 Up to RM200,000 RM20 RM5,000 (RM10,000 with SPKK)
G2 Up to RM500,000 RM80 RM25,000
G3 Up to RM1,000,000 RM150 RM50,000
G4 Up to RM3,000,000 RM350 RM150,000
G5 Up to RM5,000,000 RM700 RM250,000
G6 Up to RM10,000,000 RM1,000 RM500,000
G7 No limit RM1,400 RM750,000

The contract limits and fees come from CIDB’s own documents; its fee schedule lists the registration fees per year. The paid-up capital figures aren’t in the CIDB pages we could read. They come from a 2019 news report of the government’s announcement and from 2026 registration guides, which agree with each other. Check the current figure in CIMS when you apply.

For a renovation firm, G1 suits single homes and small shops. If you regularly quote whole landed houses or office fit-outs above RM200,000, plan for G2.

What CIDB G1 registration involves

You apply online through CIMS (cims.cidb.gov.my), and the application is submitted by an owner or director. One person can apply for only one company.

  1. Register the business with SSM first. CIDB registers local contractors with at least 70% local equity.
  2. Prepare your technical person. 2026 registration guides say G1 to G3 need one Malaysian holding a relevant technical certificate where available. If you have none, the owner or a director must later pass CIDB’s business management course (SKP) before the first renewal.
  3. Pay the RM50 processing fee within 7 days of submitting, or the application is cancelled.
  4. Pay the registration fee within 14 days of the approval letter, or the approval lapses. Fees aren’t refunded.
  5. Print your certificate (PPK) online. There’s no counter collection.

New contractors start with two default specialisations: B04 (general building) and CE21 (civil engineering). After registering, one owner or director must attend the Integrity and Code of Ethics course within 2 years, or before the next renewal if that comes first. CIDB may also ask a G1 contractor to hold an MCORE rating before the next renewal.

If you want government work, you also need the SPKK certificate, which has no registration fee but needs a valid PPK. Bumiputera firms can apply for the STB status certificate in the same system.

Specialisation codes for renovation work

Beyond B04, CIDB adds specialisations when you show a letter of award for that kind of work or a CIDB skills certificate. A 2026 list of CIDB codes includes these that renovation contractors and interior designers use most:

Code Work
B04 General building construction
B07 Interior decoration, including ceilings and partitions
B08 Waterproofing
B13 Tiling
B14 Painting
B18 Metal works, such as grilles and awnings
B26 Demolition
B28 Renovation: additions and alterations to buildings
E04 Low-voltage electrical installation and wiring

Some codes need another licence as well. Electrical wiring needs registration with the Energy Commission, and internal plumbing (B10) needs a permit from the water regulator, SPAN. Each change to your codes costs a RM30 processing fee in CIMS.

Keeping your registration valid

  • Renew before expiry. Renewal costs a RM30 processing fee plus 50% of your grade’s registration fee if your grade stays the same. The renewal period is 1 to 3 years, depending on your CCD points.
  • Collect CCD points. CIDB requires registered contractors to take part in its Continuous Contractor Development programme. The points held by owners, directors and staff decide how long your next registration runs.
  • Stay active. A contractor with no activity for 3 years in a row can have the certificate revoked.
  • Declare projects. Submit project details to CIDB within 14 days of being awarded a job.
  • Show your number on site. Display your CIDB registration number on a signboard at each site, and make sure site workers hold a valid Construction Personnel Card (the CIDB “green card”).

CIDB on your quotation

Your registration is part of what a client checks before signing, so put it where they can see it:

  • Show your CIDB registration number and grade next to your SSM number on every quotation. Clients can look it up on the CIMS portal.
  • Check the grade limit against the contract sum, including likely variations, before you quote a large job.
  • Mention the CIDB levy on big contracts. CIDB charges a levy of 0.125% on construction contracts above RM500,000, settled by the main contractor who declares the project. On a RM600,000 contract, for example, the levy is RM750 (illustrative). Most G1 jobs are below the threshold.
  • Use a recognised contract. CIDB’s free Standard Terms of Construction Contract for Renovation Work and Small Projects has no minimum or maximum value, and pairs well with an itemised quotation.

Frequently asked questions

Do renovation contractors need CIDB registration in Malaysia?
Generally yes. Section 25 of the CIDB Act 1994 (Act 520) requires every contractor who carries out construction works to register with CIDB, and CIDB defines construction works to include repair, maintenance, alteration and renovation. The CIDB documents we reviewed set no minimum job value, so check with CIDB if you think an exemption applies.
What is the CIDB G1 limit?
A G1 contractor can tender for or carry out work worth up to RM200,000 per contract, according to CIDB's registration scope document. Above that you need a higher grade, starting with G2 for work up to RM500,000.
How much does CIDB G1 registration cost?
CIDB charges a RM50 processing fee for a new registration, paid online within 7 days of applying, and a G1 registration fee of RM20, which its fee schedule lists per year. Renewal costs a RM30 processing fee plus half the registration fee if your grade doesn't change.
What is the penalty for working without CIDB registration?
Under Section 29 of Act 520, a contractor convicted of carrying out construction work without registering can be fined from RM10,000 to RM100,000. CIDB can also issue a written notice under Section 30 to stop the work.
How long is a CIDB registration valid?
A new registration is valid for up to 2 years from the date you pay the fee. Renewals run for 1 to 3 years, depending on how many continuous development (CCD) points your company has collected.
